body: Generation 4 coverage was captured with red and white pickup trucks, which are well blurred.
The Generation 3 Google car in Iceland is a white car with a long antenna.
Icelandic licence plates are fully white with blue characters and lack the blue EU strip. The blue characters can be hard to see through the blur.
Iceland has unique yellow bollards with a white reflector, which are extremely common on rural roads.
Iceland's landscape is often barren and treeless with dark grey soil from volcanic rocks. The lack of trees makes it unique in Northern Europe.
Iceland is a geologically active country with rugged, mountainous landscapes shaped by volcanoes. You can find unique features like geothermal lakes, lava fields, and rift valleys.
Icelandic road direction signs are yellow, often with a white inset box for road numbers. A dashed border on the inset box indicates a nearby road.
Icelandic pedestrian signs have four stripes and a yellow background, which is unique in Europe.
The Icelandic language uses unique letters like ð, þ, and æ, and vowels with acute accents. The letter ð is also in Faroese, and æ is in Danish, Norwegian, and Faroese.
Icelandic street signs have a white background, black text, and often a thin metal rim. They are usually attached to lampposts or traffic lights.
Iceland has all-white road lines and no yellow road lines. If outside lines are present, they are solid or dashed.
Icelandic chevrons have yellow arrows on a black background, similar to Norway and Finland.
Icelandic warning signs have a yellow background, similar to Sweden and Finland.
Iceland's Street View coverage is sparse, with the densest coverage in the southwest. Few interior roads are covered.
Iceland's road numbering system is region-specific. The main ring road is number 1, and the first digit of other roads (2-9) follows a clockwise pattern around the island starting from the south.
The Westfjords region is characterized by narrow fjords surrounded by moderately tall, flat-topped mountains.
The Eastfjords are distinguished from the Westfjords by their larger and more jagged mountains.
The area west of Akureyri has many north-facing valleys between tall, often snow-capped peaks.
The inland regions of Iceland, especially in the east, are barren landscapes of dark volcanic gravel with little vegetation.
The Southwest of Iceland is a relatively flat farmland landscape with numerous farmsteads and distant mountains.
The wide valley around Eiðar is hilly and agricultural, with tall, snowy peaks visible to the east and northwest.
The valley near Hallormsstaður has low-lying mountains, a wide river, and an unusual amount of trees for Iceland.
The area near Selfoss is recognizable by a distinct flat-ridge mountain visible from a wide, flat area.
Reykjavík, the capital, is by far the largest city in Iceland, feeling much more urban than other cities. It is mostly flat and located on a bay.
Akureyri, the second-largest city, is in a north-south valley with recognizable mountains to the east and west.
The Gen 4 pickup truck color can indicate the region: red trucks in the southwest and white trucks in the northeast.
Impressive glaciers from the Vatnajökull ice cap are visible from the ring road on the southern coast.
Only a few highways in Iceland are divided or have more than two lanes, mostly located around Reykjavík.
The island of Heimaey is recognizable by its ragged rocky cliffs overlooking the main town.
Very foggy coverage is common around the town of Bakkagerði in northeastern Iceland.
